zebralogic.title: Consolidate Direct Equivalences
zebralogic.principle: When a clue directly equates two attributes (e.g., "the associate degree holder is the cruise lover"), merge them into a single combined identity. This reduces the search space by treating the linked attributes as one unit.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: Whenever a clue states that two attribute values refer to the same person.
zebralogic.example: Treating "associate degree" and "cruise" as separate when the clue says they belong to the same individual.

zebralogic.title: Assign Fixed Positions Immediately
zebralogic.principle: If a clue fixes an attribute to a specific house number, place it right away and propagate the resulting constraints. Early placement prevents unnecessary branching.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue mentions a concrete house index (e.g., "the mountain vacation is in house 5").
zebralogic.example: Delaying the placement of "mountain" to house 5 and treating it as a variable during the search.

zebralogic.title: Translate 'N houses between' to Exact Distance
zebralogic.principle: Convert "there are N houses between X and Y" into the exact distance constraint |pos(X) − pos(Y)| = N + 1. This removes ambiguity about ordering.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue specifies a numeric gap between two attributes.
zebralogic.example: Interpreting "two houses between" as merely "X is left of Y" and allowing a gap of any size.

zebralogic.title: Enforce Adjacency for 'next to' and Ordered Left
zebralogic.principle: Translate "next to" into an adjacency constraint (|pos(A) − pos(B)| = 1) and "directly left of" into ordered adjacency (pos(A) = pos(B) − 1). This captures the exact spatial relationship required by the clue.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue uses adjacency language such as "next to" or "directly left of".
zebralogic.example: Treating "directly left of" as just "to the left of" and allowing empty houses in between.

zebralogic.title: Treat Consecutive Chains as a Block
zebralogic.principle: When several adjacency clues form a sequence (e.g., A left of B left of C), treat the whole chain as a single block. This fixes the relative order of the involved houses and cuts down permutations.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When three or more attributes are linked by ordered adjacency clues.
zebralogic.example: Considering each adjacency separately and missing the fact that the chain forces a fixed ordering of the three houses.

zebralogic.title: Propagate Linked Attribute Pairs
zebralogic.principle: Whenever two attributes are linked by a clue (e.g., "Alice is German"), immediately propagate that link to all other constraints. This prevents contradictory assignments later on.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: After establishing a direct equivalence between two attribute values.
zebralogic.example: Failing to propagate that "Alice" is "german", leading to a later clue that forces "German" elsewhere.

zebralogic.title: Output Solution in Expected JSON Table Format
zebralogic.principle: Produce a JSON object with top‑level keys "header" (list of column names) and "rows" (list of rows), using the exact attribute strings and order required by the verifier.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: At the very end of the response, after any reasoning.
zebralogic.example: Returning a plain‑text table or omitting the "header" key, causing the verifier to reject the answer.

zebralogic.title: Keep Reasoning Concise to Avoid Token Truncation
zebralogic.principle: Limit explanatory text so the final JSON is not cut off; place the solution near the end of the output. This ensures the verifier receives the complete answer.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: Throughout the response, especially for larger puzzles where the token budget is tight.
zebralogic.example: Writing a long paragraph before the JSON, causing the JSON to be truncated and omitted from the verifier's parsing.

zebralogic.title: Preserve Original Attribute Tokens (Case and Spelling)
zebralogic.principle: Copy attribute values verbatim from the problem statement, preserving their exact case, spelling, and any abbreviations. The verifier matches strings literally, so any deviation (e.g., capitalising or using synonyms) leads to rejection.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When constructing the final JSON rows for each house.
zebralogic.example: Writing "German" instead of the required "german" or "British" instead of "brit", which makes the answer mismatched.

zebralogic.description: Generating overly long reasoning before the final answer, causing the output to exceed the token limit and truncate the JSON solution.
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model tries to be thorough and writes extensive explanations, forgetting the fixed token budget of a single‑turn task.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Keep the reasoning brief and place the JSON solution near the end of the response.

zebralogic.description: Providing the solution in a format not recognized by the verifier (e.g., missing "header"/"rows" keys or adding extra wrapper fields).
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model misremembers the exact output schema required for zebra‑logic puzzles.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Always output a JSON object with exactly the keys "header" and "rows", matching the column order expected by the verifier.

zebralogic.description: Using incorrect case or synonyms for attribute values (e.g., "German" instead of "german").
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model assumes attribute strings are case‑insensitive or tries to make them look more natural.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Copy attribute tokens verbatim from the problem description, preserving case and spelling exactly.
